title: What Makes a Career Fulfilling? Beyond Salary and Status
paragraphs: When people are asked what they want from their careers, the answers that feature most prominently are often not the ones that economic theory would predict. Yes, people want to be paid fairly — below a certain income level, financial stress undermines everything else. But study after study has found that once basic financial security is achieved, the factors that drive job satisfaction are primarily non-financial: the quality of relationships at work, the sense of autonomy and control over one's tasks, the opportunity to grow and develop, and — most powerfully — the sense of purpose and meaning.

This finding, often associated with psychologist Frederick Herzberg's "two-factor theory" of motivation, distinguishes between "hygiene factors" and "motivators." Hygiene factors — salary, working conditions, job security — do not generate satisfaction when present; they merely prevent dissatisfaction. Motivators — recognition, achievement, responsibility, and personal growth — are what actually drive engagement and fulfilment. A person with an excellent salary but no autonomy or recognition is not satisfied; they are merely not actively miserable.

The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi described the experience of deep engagement with meaningful work as "flow" — a state of complete absorption in a challenging activity where time seems to stop and performance is at its peak. Flow occurs when the level of challenge is well-matched to the level of skill: too easy, and the work becomes boring; too hard, and it becomes anxiety-inducing. The conditions that produce flow — clear goals, immediate feedback, and an optimal level of challenge — are the conditions of genuinely engaging work.

In recent years, the concept of "ikigai" — a Japanese word roughly translating as "reason for being" — has attracted attention in discussions of work and purpose. Ikigai is found at the intersection of four elements: what you love, what you are good at, what the world needs, and what you can be paid for. A career that combines all four is, in this framework, one that is both personally fulfilling and socially valuable. The framework is useful not just as a goal but as a diagnostic tool: someone who feels unfulfilled can ask themselves which of these four elements is missing from their current work.

Research into what makes careers fulfilling has also highlighted the importance of relationships and community. People who feel genuinely connected to their colleagues — who experience their workplace as a community, not merely a transactional exchange of labour for pay — report significantly higher levels of engagement and wellbeing. Loneliness and isolation at work are associated with lower productivity, higher turnover, and worse mental health outcomes. Building and maintaining meaningful professional relationships is therefore not a soft, peripheral concern — it is central to career fulfilment and organisational success.

A persistent challenge in discussions of career fulfilment is the tension between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. Extrinsic motivation — doing something for external rewards such as pay, status, or recognition — is real and important. But research consistently shows that over-reliance on extrinsic motivation can crowd out intrinsic motivation — the desire to do something because it is interesting, challenging, or meaningful in itself. This is particularly relevant in careers where creative or complex work is central: paying someone more to do creative work does not necessarily make them do it better, and may even make them more narrowly focused on the reward rather than the work itself.

None of this is to say that salary does not matter, or that people should pursue passion regardless of economic reality. Economic constraints are real, and a poorly-paid job, however meaningful, creates its own forms of stress and vulnerability. The most realistic framework for career decision-making integrates both dimensions: building towards work that is both personally meaningful and economically sustainable, and recognising that this is usually a journey rather than a single choice.
